questions.question: For a maximization problem with objective $f$ and feasible set $F$, which condition makes a vector $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ an optimal solution?
options: $\boldsymbol{x}^*\in F$ and $f(\boldsymbol{x}^*)\le f(\boldsymbol{x})$ for every $\boldsymbol{x}\in F$
$f(\boldsymbol{x}^*)$ is the largest value of $f$ over all vectors, feasible or not
$\boldsymbol{x}^*\in F$ and $f(\boldsymbol{x}^*)>f(\boldsymbol{x})$ for every other $\boldsymbol{x}\in F$
$\boldsymbol{x}^*\in F$ and $f(\boldsymbol{x}^*)\ge f(\boldsymbol{x})$ for every $\boldsymbol{x}\in F$

questions.question: For an LP that maximizes $z=4x_1+x_2$, the plan $x_1=5$, $x_2=2$ is feasible with $z=22$, and no feasible plan gives a larger $z$. Which description uses the terms correctly?
options: 22 is the optimal solution and $(5,2)$ is the optimal value.
$(5,2)$ is the optimal solution, so no other plan can reach 22.
$(5,2)$ is an optimal solution, and 22 is the optimal value.
$x_1=5$ is the optimal solution and $x_2=2$ is a feasible one.

questions.question: For a profit-maximization model, plan A satisfies every constraint and earns 50, while plan B violates one capacity constraint and earns 60. No other plans have been examined. What can be concluded?
options: B is optimal, since its higher profit outweighs one violated constraint.
B is not optimal; A must still be compared with all feasible plans.
A is optimal, since it is the best feasible plan examined so far.
The optimal value is 60, even though plan B itself is not allowed.

questions.question: A production LP has optimal solution $\boldsymbol{x}^*$. The available machine hours are then cut, and $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ now needs more machine hours than are available. What follows for the new model?
options: $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ stays optimal, since the objective function has not changed.
$\boldsymbol{x}^*$ stays optimal, but the optimal value drops with the hours.
The new optimum is always $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ scaled down to fit the hours.
$\boldsymbol{x}^*$ is now infeasible, so it cannot be optimal for the new data.

questions.question: A cost-minimization model has constraints that no decision can satisfy at the same time, so its feasible set $F$ is empty. What can be said about an optimal solution $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ of this model?
options: Producing nothing is optimal, since it incurs no cost at all.
There is none, since any optimal solution must belong to $F$.
The minimizer of the cost, ignoring the constraints, is optimal.
Every vector is optimal, since there is nothing to compare with.

questions.question: A farm must choose one of four feed plans $(x_1,x_2)$, in tonnes of two feeds, to minimize cost $5x_1+2x_2$; a plan is allowed only if $2x_1+x_2\ge8$. The plans are $(1,5)$, $(1,6)$, $(3,2)$ and $(4,4)$. Which plan is optimal?
options: $(1,6)$, with cost 17
$(1,5)$, with cost 15
$(3,2)$, with cost 19
$(4,4)$, with cost 28

questions.question: For the LP maximize $2x_1+3x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\le6$, $x_2\le4$ and $x_1,x_2\ge0$, a student claims that $(3,3)$, with value 15, is optimal. Which assessment is correct?
options: Not optimal: $(2,4)$ is feasible with value 16.
Optimal, since it satisfies every constraint.
Optimal, since it lies on the line $x_1+x_2=6$.
Not optimal: $(0,6)$ is better, with value 18.

questions.question: A one-variable model minimizes $f(x)=2x-3$ over the feasible set $F=\{x\colon 1\le x\le4\}$. What are the optimal solution and the optimal value?
options: $x^*=4$, with optimal value $5$
$x^*=-1$, the smallest value of $f$
$x^*=1$, with optimal value $-1$
$x^*=1.5$, where $f(x)$ equals $0$

questions.question: A model minimizes $f(x)=(x-3)^2+1$ subject to $x\ge5$. What are the optimal solution $x^*$ and the optimal value $z^*$?
options: No $x^*$: $f$ grows without limit

questions.question: For the LP maximize $x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1-x_2\le2$ and $x_1,x_2\ge0$, which statement about an optimal solution is correct?
options: $(2,0)$, where $x_1-x_2=2$ meets $x_2=0$, is optimal with value 2.
$(0,0)$ is optimal with value 0, as it satisfies every constraint.
An optimal solution exists, since the feasible set is nonempty.
None exists: $(t,t)$ is feasible with value $2t$ for all $t\ge0$.

questions.question: In a maximization model with objective $f$ and feasible set $F$, both $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ and $\boldsymbol{y}^*$ are optimal solutions. What must be true of $f(\boldsymbol{x}^*)$ and $f(\boldsymbol{y}^*)$?
options: They may differ, as long as both beat every other feasible value.
They are equal, since each one is at least as large as the other.
They are equal only if $\boldsymbol{x}^*=\boldsymbol{y}^*$, as optima are unique.
Nothing, since optimality concerns the vectors, not their values.

questions.question: An analyst generates 1000 random production plans, keeps the ones that satisfy every constraint and reports the most profitable of these as the optimal solution of a profit-maximization model. Is this report justified?
options: Yes; with 1000 plans examined, the best one is certain to be optimal.
Yes, provided the reported plan satisfies every constraint of the model.
No; an optimal plan must beat every feasible plan, not just sampled ones.
No; random plans are never feasible, so no conclusion can be drawn.

questions.question: In an optimal plan of a profit-maximization LP for two products, 10 of the 40 available finishing hours are unused. Does the unused finishing time show that the plan is not optimal?
options: No; another limit may block extra output, so an optimum can leave hours spare.
Yes; unused hours can always be turned into extra profit by producing more.
Yes; an optimal plan must use every available resource completely, with no slack.
No, but only because the objective function does not contain finishing time.

questions.question: For the LP maximize $x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\le4$, $x_1\le4$ and $x_1,x_2\ge0$, one analyst reports $(1,3)$ and another reports $(4,0)$ as an optimal solution. Which assessment is correct?
options: Only $(4,0)$ is optimal, since it also makes the limit $x_1\le4$ tight.
Neither is optimal, because an optimal solution must be unique.
Neither is optimal, since $(4,4)$ is feasible with the larger value 8.
Both: each is feasible with value 4, and no feasible point exceeds 4.

questions.question: For the constraints $x_1+x_2\le4$, $x_1\le3$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$, the plan $(3,1)$ is optimal when maximizing $3x_1+2x_2$. If the objective is changed to $x_1+2x_2$ with the same constraints, is $(3,1)$ still optimal?
options: Yes: the constraints are the same, so the optimum stays put.
No: $(0,4)$ is feasible and gives 8, more than its value 5.
Yes, though its optimal value is now 5 instead of 11.
No: $(3,1)$ has become infeasible and must be replaced.

questions.question: A budget of 10 may fund any set of four projects: A costs 6 and returns 10, B costs 5 and returns 7, C costs 5 and returns 7, D costs 4 and returns 3. Returns add up, total cost must stay within 10, and the total return is maximized. What is the optimal value?
The model minimize $f(x)=\frac{1}{x}$ subject to $x\ge1$ has $f(x)>0$ for every feasible $x$, and $f(x)$ comes arbitrarily close to 0 as $x$ grows. Does it have an optimal solution?
options: No; each feasible $x$ is beaten by $x+1$, so no smallest value is attained.
Yes, $x^*=1$, the boundary point where the feasible set begins.
Yes, with optimal value 0, attained as $x$ tends to infinity.
No, because the feasible set $\{x\colon x\ge1\}$ is unbounded.

questions.question: A maximization model with objective $f$ has optimal solution $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ and optimal value $z^*$. The objective is replaced by $g(\boldsymbol{x})=2f(\boldsymbol{x})+100$, with the same constraints. What happens?
options: Nothing changes: the same optimal solutions and the same optimal value $z^*$.
The optimal solution changes, since any change in the objective moves it.
The optimal solutions stay the same; the optimal value becomes $2z^*+100$.
The optimal solution becomes $2\boldsymbol{x}^*$, with value $2z^*+100$.

questions.question: For the LP maximize $3x_1+2x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\le5$, $x_1\le2$ and $x_1,x_2\ge0$, the feasible point $(2,3)$ has value 12. Which observation proves that $(2,3)$ is optimal?
options: At $(2,3)$ both $x_1+x_2\le5$ and $x_1\le2$ hold with equality.
$(2,3)$ beats its feasible neighbours $(2,2)$, $(1,4)$ and $(1,3)$.
Every feasible point has $3x_1+2x_2=2(x_1+x_2)+x_1\le2\cdot5+2=12$.
No feasible point has both coordinates larger than those of $(2,3)$.

questions.question: For the LP minimize $4x_1+3x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\ge10$, $x_2\le6$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$ ($x_j$ = tonnes bought from supplier $j$), the optimum is $(4,6)$ with cost 34. The limit $x_2\le6$ is raised to $x_2\le8$. What is now optimal?
options: $(4,6)$, cost 34: it is still feasible, so it stays optimal
$(2,8)$, cost 32: shift more to the cheaper supplier
$(0,10)$, cost 30: the cheaper supplier covers it all
$(4,8)$, cost 40: the larger limit is used on top
